name: Mobility drill
pattern: Slow, controlled movement of a joint through its full comfortable range, repeated for reps, usually as a warm-up.
setup: Warm, clear space; a mat for floor drills.
Start in the drill's base position: standing, half kneeling, on hands and feet, or lying.
Know your range: move to a firm stretch, never into pain.

steps.text: Step one foot far forward into a deep lunge, hands down inside the front foot.
Drop the inside elbow toward the front instep, back knee off the floor.
Open the chest and reach the inside arm to the ceiling, eyes follow the hand.
Hands down, shift the hips back and straighten the front leg.
Step back to standing or into the next lunge on the other side.

cues.why: Controlled dynamic stretching improves range and later power; fast ballistic swings help less.

cues.cue: Go a little further each rep, always pain-free.
cues.why: Range gains come from lower muscle-tendon stiffness built up over repeated reps.

cues.cue: Use 5-10 reps per drill before training.
cues.why: Dynamic drills in a warm-up raise range without the short-term strength loss of long static holds.

cues.cue: Brace lightly so the joint you are training does the moving.
cues.why: If the low back moves instead, the target joint (hip, shoulder, upper back) gets less range.

cues.cue: Nerve glides: gentle, no tingling that lasts.
cues.why: Sliders move the nerve with little strain; tensioners stretch it and are harder on an irritated nerve.

breathing: Breathe out as you move into the end range, in as you return.

tempo.note: About 2 s into the range, a short pause, 2 s back; 5-10 reps per side.

mistakes.name: Bouncing at end range
mistakes.looks: Fast swings or jerks at the end of the movement.
mistakes.fix: Slow down and pause for a breath at the end.
mistakes.why: Ballistic swings give less benefit and more strain than controlled moves.

mistakes.name: Low back does the work
mistakes.looks: In lunges and leg swings the low back arches or rounds instead of the hip moving.
mistakes.fix: Squeeze the back glute, ribs down, smaller range.
mistakes.why: The hip stays stiff and the spine takes the range.

mistakes.name: Front knee caves in
mistakes.looks: In the lunge or squat drills the knee falls inside the foot.
mistakes.fix: Knee over the second toe, foot flat.
mistakes.why: Loads the inside of the knee.

safety: Jefferson curls (loaded spine rounding): start with bodyweight, add load very slowly, skip with disc problems or osteoporosis.
Nerve glides: stop if tingling or numbness lasts after the drill.
Recent joint injury or surgery: follow your physio's range limits.

variants.change: Light load adds a pull into the range; keep it slow.
Band, stick or wall guides the path; same joint range.
Same drill, a different step in the sequence or a different view.

easier: hands on a box or chair

subtypes.name: Nerve glides
subtypes.change: Seated; move two joints in opposite directions so the nerve slides, e.g. tip the head toward the arm as the wrist bends back, then reverse. Sciatic: knee straightens as the head lifts.

subtypes.name: Jefferson curl
subtypes.change: Standing on a step, legs straight, roll down one vertebra at a time from the head, then roll up. Light load in the hands.

subtypes.name: Pelvic tilts
subtypes.change: Lying with knees bent (or standing), tip the pelvis to flatten the low back, then arch it gently. 'Into bridge' rolls on up into a bridge.

subtypes.name: Lunge flows, world's greatest stretch
subtypes.match: greatest|in lunge|kneeling to|half kneeling(?! halo)|side lunge|knee down|butt walking
subtypes.change: Deep lunge flows that open the hip flexor, adductor and upper back in one sequence; half-kneeling and kneeling-to-stand drills train the transitions.

subtypes.name: Squat mobility
subtypes.change: Sink into a deep squat, heels down, chest up; pry the knees out with the elbows, shift side to side, stand up. Overhead version holds a stick overhead.

subtypes.name: Good morning (hinge drill)
subtypes.change: Hands behind the head or a stick on the back, soft knees; push the hips back with a flat back until the hamstrings stretch, then stand.

subtypes.name: Inchworm, plank to down dog
subtypes.change: From standing, fold and walk the hands out to a plank, then walk the feet up to the hands with straight legs.

subtypes.name: Leg swings and hip circles
subtypes.match: leg circle|figure 8|half circle|leg swing|front kick|hip circle
subtypes.change: Standing tall holding a support (or lying), swing or circle one leg through a smooth, growing range; the trunk stays still.

subtypes.name: Knee circles and patella
subtypes.change: Feet together, knees soft, hands on the knees; circle the knees. Patella: seated, leg relaxed, glide the kneecap gently with the fingers.

subtypes.name: Upper-back rotation
subtypes.match: side to side knee|windmill|archer|push through|diagonal reach|wring|headbanger
subtypes.change: Turn the rib cage while the pelvis stays put: lying knee drops side to side, standing windmill or archer reach, or a reach-through from all fours.

subtypes.name: Shoulder circles, halos, stick raises
subtypes.match: halo|around the world|front raise|overhead|phelps|warming up|military press|floor slide|ballerina|clap|shrug
subtypes.change: Move the arms through a full overhead circle: halos pass a light weight around the head; stick raises lift a dowel from the hips to overhead; floor slides keep the arms on the floor like a snow angel.

motion.basis: Default flow is the world's greatest stretch. No kinematic study of these drills was found; angles are estimates kept within adult normal ranges from soucie2011 (hip extension about 17°, shoulder flexion about 170°, ankle dorsiflexion about 13° unloaded, more when loaded in a lunge). Dosing and speed cues from opplert2018 and behm2011. Subtypes are grouped by joint and listed most specific first; the first match wins. trunkRot (+ toward the right) is an extra key not yet in the README convention.

sources.cite: Opplert J, Babault N. Acute effects of dynamic stretching on muscle flexibility and performance: an analysis of the current literature. Sports Med. 2018;48(2):299-325.
